In the shadow of a founding document
item.description:
On the evening of 17 October, the seminar room of the Liberation War Museum in Dhaka became more than a screening venue.
It turned into a meeting place of history, memory, and reflection.
People from different professions and generations gathered there to attend the premiere of The Birth of a Unique Book , the latest documentary by eminent filmmaker Tanvir Mokammel.
Organized by Ayner Kotha , an organization working to increase public awareness about citizens' rights, the event was marked by appealing simplicity.
There were no lengthy speeches, no elaborate ceremonies, and no attempt to overwhelm the audience with formality. The focus remained firmly on the documentary itself and on the remarkable story it sought to tell: the birth, evolution, and continuing significance of Bangladesh's 1972 Constitution.
Before the screening, Mokammel delivered a brief introductory address.
Standing at the podium, he explained the motivation behind the project. What struck me most was the modesty of his claim.
The documentary, he noted, did not seek to discover any new facts or advance a novel interpretation of history. Rather, it aimed to revisit existing documents, archival material, and eyewitness accounts in order to reconstruct the process through which the Constitution of Bangladesh came into being.
As the lights dimmed and the documentary began, it became clear that the film was about much more than a legal document.
It was about the journey of a people towards self-determination.
One of the documentary's greatest strengths lies in its careful reconstruction of the historical background against which the Constitution was written. Rather than treating the Constitution as an isolated legal text, the film situates it within a long history of political struggles, aspirations, and sacrifices.
The narrative takes viewers back to the Lahore Resolution of 1940 and the debates surrounding its interpretation. It traces the tensions that emerged within Pakistan's two wings and moves through the Language Movement, the authoritarian rule of Ayub Khan, the Six-Point Movement, the mass uprising of 1969, and the watershed elections of 1970.
The documentary then follows the chain of events that culminated in the Liberation War of 1971 and the emergence of Bangladesh as an independent state on 16 December of that year.
Seen in this broader context, the Constitution appears not merely as a legal framework but as the culmination of decades of political struggle and collective aspiration.
What impressed me throughout the film was its restraint. Historical documentaries often rely heavily on dramatic narration or a rapid succession of archival footage to maintain audience interest.
Mokammel adopts a different strategy.
Photographs and video clips are certainly used, but sparingly. They are supplemented and often illuminated by interviews with individuals who either participated directly in the constitutional process or observed the formative years of the nation from positions of proximity.
The result is a documentary that invites engagement rather than demanding it through spectacle.
Among the most compelling moments were the interviews with people whose lives intersected closely with the making of the Constitution.
The presence of Dr Kamal Hossain, who led the committee responsible for drafting the Constitution, lends the film a rare historical immediacy.
Listening to him discuss those formative months, one is reminded that constitutions are not abstract texts produced in a vacuum.
They are negotiated, debated, and shaped by individuals responding to the needs and dreams of a specific historical moment.
The documentary also features the reflections of Barrister Amir-ul Islam, one of the committee's members, alongside those of economist Rehman Sobhan, who worked closely with Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman.
Their recollections help transform distant history into something tangible and human. Through their words, the audience gains insight into the urgency, idealism, and challenges that accompanied the drafting process.
Perhaps one of the most remarkable facts highlighted by the film is the speed with which the Constitution was prepared and adopted.
Bangladesh, devastated by war and burdened with the immense tasks of reconstruction, succeeded in drafting and adopting its Constitution within nine months.
The film reminds viewers that Pakistan took nearly nine years to adopt a constitution, while the process in India extended over approximately three years.
Such comparisons help underscore what an extraordinary achievement the constitutional project represented in the context of post-war Bangladesh.
Yet the documentary does not lapse into uncritical celebration. It acknowledges that constitutions are living documents shaped by changing political realities.
Consequently, a massive portion of the film examines some of the major constitutional amendments that have altered the nation's foundational text over the decades.
The Fourth Amendment, the Fifth Amendment, the Eighth Amendment, and later amendments relating to the caretaker government system are all discussed.
What makes this discussion particularly valuable is the range of voices included in it. The documentary brings together legal experts, economists, human rights advocates, and representatives of diverse social groups.
Human rights activists such as Hamida Hossain and Shirin Huq, among others, offer thoughtful assessments of the Constitution's strengths and limitations.
Some interviewees identify areas where the Constitution has not fully met the aspirations of all citizens. Others draw attention to unresolved questions concerning rights, representation, or governance.
Yet despite their differences, a broad consensus emerges from the interviews: the 1972 Constitution remains an exceptionally important and progressive foundation for Bangladesh.
As an observer, I was struck by the balance the documentary achieves.
It neither romanticises the Constitution nor dismisses its shortcomings. Instead, it encourages viewers to recognise both its historic significance and the continuing responsibility of citizens to engage with it critically. In doing so, the film embodies a democratic spirit.
Respect for a constitution does not require unquestioning reverence; rather, it involves understanding its origins, evaluating its evolution, and ensuring that its principles remain meaningful in contemporary society.
Beyond the documentary itself, the atmosphere of the premiere was noteworthy.
The audience comprised individuals from varied backgrounds, including lawyers, academics, activists, students, and members of the cultural community. There was an unmistakable sense that the screening represented more than a film event. It was also an occasion for reflection on the ideals that shaped the nation.
Particularly memorable was the sight of several distinguished figures whose contributions have become part of Bangladesh's intellectual and public life.
Dr Kamal Hossain was present, accompanied by his daughter, the prominent lawyer Sara Hossain. Economist Rehman Sobhan, Justice Ashraful Alam, human rights activist Hamida Hossain, social activist Khushi Kabir, Meghna Guhathakurta, and many others attended the program.
Their presence served as a reminder that the history explored on screen was not entirely remote. Some of the individuals who participated in, witnessed, or shaped key moments of that history were sitting among the audience, watching those memories return through film.
There was something quietly moving about this convergence of generations.
In one sense, the documentary looks backward, revisiting events that occurred more than five decades ago. Yet the audience itself symbolised continuity between past and present.
Younger viewers encountered stories they had not lived through, while older attendees revisited experiences that had helped define their lives.
The film therefore functioned not merely as a historical account but also as an intergenerational conversation.
Walking out of the auditorium after the screening, I found myself thinking about how rarely ordinary citizens engage with constitutions.
Most people encounter them only indirectly, through political debates, court rulings, or public controversies. Yet constitutions shape everyday life in profound ways.
They define the relationship between citizens and the state, articulate collective values, and establish the framework within which democratic life unfolds.
By tracing the birth and transformation of Bangladesh's Constitution, Mokammel's documentary encourages viewers to see this foundational document not as a distant legal text but as a living part of the national story.
The title, The Birth of a Unique Book , is therefore particularly apt.
The Constitution is indeed a book, but one unlike any other. It records not merely laws but aspirations. It embodies the hopes of a nation emerging from war and seeking to define itself.
The documentary reminds us that behind every article and clause lies the memory of historical struggles, political debates, and human choices.
In the end, the greatest achievement of Mokammel's film may be its ability to make constitutional history accessible without oversimplifying it.
It succeeds as a work of historical documentation, but it also succeeds as an invitation to reflection.
By bringing together archival material, eyewitness testimony, and thoughtful analysis, it encourages viewers to revisit questions about citizenship, democracy, rights, and the kind of society Bangladesh aspires to become.
The evening at the Liberation War Museum thus felt significant not because a new documentary was unveiled, but because it reopened a conversation about the nation's founding values.
In a time when public discourse is often fragmented and polarized, The Birth of a Unique Book offers something rare: an opportunity to look back at a foundational moment in Bangladesh's history and to consider, with humility and seriousness, what that legacy means today.
Ahmed Ahsanuzzaman is professor of English and Director, Kazi Nazrul Islam and Abbasuddin Ahmed Research & Study Centre at Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB).

item.title: Tahsif's female friend placed on 4-day remand in murder case
item.description:
A Dhaka court has placed a female friend of former Air Force official Tahsif Souri on a four-day police remand in a murder case filed over his death.
Inspector Md Firoz Uddin, the investigation officer of the case filed with Uttara East Police Station, sought a seven-day remand to question her.
Following the hearing, Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Ripon Hossain granted a four-day remand.
In the remand petition, the investigation officer said she was suspected of being involved in the incident.
State prosecutor Shamsuddoha Sumon argued in favour of the remand, saying investigators needed to cross-check her statements against information provided by another accused, Ahmed Shahriar Reza Dip, who is already on remand.
He sought the maximum remand period in the interest of a proper investigation.
Defence lawyer Imam Hossain Javed opposed the remand and sought bail, arguing that she had no involvement in the killing.
He said Dip was the main accused named in the case and that Tahsif Souri’s female friend had been arrested solely on the basis of CCTV footage. According to the lawyer, Souri had dropped her off at her home in his car around midnight that night, after which they had no further contact.
He added that the two had gone to a restaurant for a meal because of their relationship, and that she knew nothing beyond that.
Tahsif's female friend was arrested from the Kafrul area around 2am on Sunday.
Earlier, on Saturday, another accused in the case, Ahmed Shahriar Reza Dip, described as a younger friend of Souri, was placed on a four-day remand for questioning.
Souri’s father, KM Enayetul Karim, filed the murder case with Uttarkhan Police Station on Friday night after his son’s body was recovered.
Souri, who came into the spotlight as the person who recorded the video of ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina leaving the country, was found floating in the Turag River near Rajabari Ghat on Wednesday afternoon. Naval police recovered his body.
He had left his home on his motorcycle on Tuesday evening after Dip called him downstairs.
Dip told reporters on Thursday that he had parted ways with Souri in the Uttara House Building area after they had dinner together at a restaurant.
That night, the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) took Dip into custody for questioning from his home on Babar Road in Mohammadpur.
Based on information provided by Dip, investigators recovered Souri’s motorcycle on Friday morning.
Dip also admitted to going with Souri to the area, which is known as a drug hotspot, late that night. PBI officials later took him to the area on Friday as part of the investigation.

item.title: Garment workers block Dhaka-Tangail highway, set police box on fire
item.description:
Garment workers blocked the Dhaka-Tangail highway in Gazipur on Sunday, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000, bringing traffic to a standstill. Five platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) were deployed to help control the situation.
A police box in Konabari was also set on fire during the unrest.
Workers began gathering on the highway shortly after 8am and blocked the road by 9:30am, disrupting traffic along the busy route.
Chanting slogans demanding higher wages, workers occupied several points along the highway, including Safipur Bazar, Chandra Polli Bidyut, Mouchak and Telichala in Kaliakair upazila.
Hundreds of workers, some carrying sticks, took positions at different points, halting traffic and causing significant hardship for passengers.
Workers from several factories, including Karani Knit Composite and Knit Asia in the Ratanpur area of Kaliakair, joined the protest instead of continuing their work.
They had initially entered their factories in the morning to mark their attendance before leaving the premises to join the demonstration near Safipur Bazar.
Several nearby factories suspended operations amid the unrest.
Iftekhar Hossain, officer-in-charge of Konabari police station under Gazipur Metropolitan Police, said protesters had set fire to a police box located in the middle of the Dhaka-Tangail highway in the Konabari area.
Shahidul Islam, officer-in-charge of Kaliakair police station, confirmed that traffic remained suspended as workers continued occupying the highway and demonstrating since Sunday morning.

item.title: Tahsif’s death: Police claim preliminary evidence against Dip
item.description:
Police have reportedly found preliminary evidence linking Ahmed Shahriar Reza Dip to the death of his friend, former Bangladesh Air Force officer KM Tahsif Souri, who is suspected to have been murdered.
Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Md Hasib Ullah Pias on Saturday placed Dip on a four-day remand in a case filed over Tahsif’s death, said Additional Public Prosecutor Muhammad Shamsud Doha Sumon.
Police had sought seven days of remand, citing preliminary findings in their petition.
“We have found preliminary evidence of Dip’s involvement in Tahsif Souri’s death. We will question him in greater detail during remand. We cannot disclose anything further at this stage in the interest of the investigation,” Abdullah Al Mamun, superintendent of police (Dhaka region) of the River Police, told The Daily Star.
A police official involved in the investigation, speaking on condition of anonymity, said CCTV footage collected from different locations showed Dip accompanying Tahsif between 6:30pm and 1:30am.
Investigators also found that Dip had accompanied Tahsif to the Mazar Basti area in Tongi but returned alone, the official said.
“This has raised questions among the investigators,” the official added, saying information obtained during preliminary questioning also pointed to Dip’s involvement.
The Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) picked up Dip from his residence on Babar Road in Mohammadpur late Thursday night. He was later shown arrested in the case filed by Tahsif’s father, KM Enayetul Karim, against unidentified persons with Uttarkhan police late Friday night.
Although registered as a murder case, the father’s written complaint did not directly accuse anyone of murder. Instead, he asked the authorities to establish the actual cause of his son’s death and take necessary action.
Tahsif, 28, left his Uttara residence on Tuesday evening and went missing. His body was recovered from the Turag river near Rajabari Ghat in Tongi the following afternoon.

item.title: Anti-state conspiracy: Major (retd) Khandaker Hafiz arrested
item.description:
The Detective Branch (DB) of Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) has arrested Major (retd) Khandaker Abdul Hafiz in a case filed over alleged anti-state conspiracy, violent incitement, illegal funding, and social media propaganda.
A DB team picked him up from the capital’s Banani area late Thursday night, said DMP Additional Commissioner (DB) Md Shafiqul Islam.
He said Hafiz was arrested in connection with the case in which two other former Army officers have already been arrested.
Shafiqul alleged that Hafiz, Lt Col (retd) Debashish Kumar Barua and Lieutenant (retd) Kazi Gulshan Ara were involved in anti-state activities.
Debashish and Gulshan Ara are currently in jail in connection with the case filed with Pallabi Police Station under several sections of the Anti-Terrorism Act and the Cyber Security Ordinance.
Earlier, DB arrested the two retired Army officers from Dhaka on the night of October 11.
It earlier claimed that it had information about their alleged links to activities of the Awami League, whose activities are currently banned, as part of an alleged conspiracy to create instability in the country.
The DB also said the two officers were arrested based on specific information about their alleged involvement in anti-state propaganda on social media and attempts to undermine public security through cybercrimes.

item.title: HC grants bail to ex-lawmaker Akhtaruzzaman in airport case
item.description:
The High Court on Sunday granted bail to former lawmaker Major (retd) Akhtaruzzaman in a case filed over allegedly obstructing government work and misbehaving with officials at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport.
A High Court bench led by Justice KM Zahid Sarwar passed the order after hearing his bail petition.
Senior lawyer Mohammad Shishir Manir appeared for Akhtaruzzaman, who was expelled from BNP several times and joined Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami in December 2025, during the hearing.
Earlier, on October 26, the Dhaka Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge Court-5 rejected his bail petition.
The Detective Branch (DB) of police arrested Akhtaruzzaman from his residence in the Dhaka Cantonment area on October 2. The following day, a court placed him on a one-day remand for interrogation.
After the remand, he was produced before a court on October 4, which rejected his bail petition and sent him to jail.
The case was filed over an incident at the airport on October 1, when passengers arriving from Madinah on a Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight faced a shortage of luggage trolleys and delays in collecting their baggage.
According to the case statement, Akhtaruzzaman allegedly verbally abused and threatened Airport Executive Director Group Captain SM Ragib Samad and assaulted security supervisor Warrant Officer Mohammad Kamal Uddin.
He was also accused of throwing bottles of Zamzam water from passengers' trolleys and behaving aggressively towards a Biman representative.

item.title: Metro rail skips three stations amid garment workers’ protests
item.description:
Metro rail services in Dhaka are operating without stopping at three stations following a request from police amid clashes between garment workers and law enforcement.
Since Sunday afternoon, trains have been bypassing Pallabi, Mirpur-11 and Mirpur-10 stations, Md Nazrul Islam, director (operations and maintenance) of Dhaka Mass Transit Company Ltd (DMTCL), confirmed to Bangla Tribune.
He said train services at the three stations had been suspended following a clash between garment workers and police around noon.
Meanwhile, a police vehicle was reportedly set on fire in the Mirpur-11 area. Hamidur Rahman, a duty officer at the Fire Service, said two firefighting units had been sent to the scene.
Police also fired tear gas shells to disperse workers in the Mirpur-10 area.
Earlier, hundreds of workers from different garment factories took to the streets around 9am, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000. The protest brought traffic in Mirpur to a standstill.
Workers and police clashed in a series of confrontations, including chases and counter-chases.
Around 11am, police charged batons and fired tear gas shells to disperse protesters in the Mirpur-10 area. Some workers were also seen throwing bricks and stones during the clashes.

item.title: Clashes in Mirpur, Gazipur and Ashulia as garment protests continue
item.description:
Protests and road blockades continued on Sunday in Mirpur in the capital, Kaliakair in Gazipur and the Savar-Ashulia industrial belt, with clashes between workers and police, vandalism and arson reported at several locations.
Garment workers began protesting at the Mirpur-10 roundabout in the morning, demanding a minimum monthly wage of Tk30,000. The demonstrations later spread to Mirpur-11, Mirpur-12 and surrounding areas.
Clashes between workers and police broke out around 11:30am and continued into the afternoon.
Vehicular movement came to a halt on several roads in Mirpur. As tensions escalated, the Mirpur-10, Mirpur-11 and Pallabi metro rail stations were temporarily closed. A police vehicle parked beneath the Mirpur-11 metro station was also set on fire during the unrest.
In Gazipur's Kaliakair upazila, workers staged demonstrations in Chandra, Palli Bidyut, Safipur, Mouchak and Konabari.
A blockade of the Dhaka-Tangail Highway disrupted traffic for nearly six hours. A garment factory warehouse and a vehicle belonging to a law enforcement agency were also reportedly set on fire.
Police fired tear gas and sound grenades to bring the situation under control. Traffic gradually returned to normal after workers left the roads.
Protests in different parts of Savar and Ashulia also disrupted traffic on the Dhaka-Aricha Highway, particularly around Hemayetpur and several other locations.
According to industrial police, 177 factories in the Savar-Ashulia industrial belt and more than 100 in Gazipur declared holidays on Sunday amid the unrest. Production was suspended at more than 300 factories in total.
Police have arrested several people in Mirpur and Gazipur on allegations of vandalism, arson and sabotage during the workers' protests.
The Mirpur division of Dhaka Metropolitan Police said 29 people had been arrested in connection with the demonstrations in the area. Industrial police, meanwhile, reported the arrest of 20 people in the Gazipur industrial zone.
Police also said nine activists and leaders of the banned Awami League and its affiliated organisations had been arrested during operations in different parts of Kaliakair upazila.
According to police, those arrested include members of the Awami League, Jubo League, Chhatra League, Krishak League and Sramik League at various levels.
Kaliakair police station Officer-in-Charge Shahidul Islam said the arrests were made following allegations that the individuals were involved in various criminal activities.
Police have also alleged political involvement in the labour unrest. However, the specific allegations against those arrested, the details of the cases filed and the evidence supporting the charges will be subject to the judicial process.
Labour Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury has alleged that some political organisations are deliberately attempting to create instability in the garment industry.
He claimed that outsiders had pelted several factories with stones and tried to mobilise workers to take to the streets.
Meanwhile, Mohammad Rashed Khan, a political assistant to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, alleged in a social media post that a Chhatra League leader had been leading a workers' protest in Gazipur. He also questioned the role of various political groups in the unrest.
Following the formation of the wage board, the labour minister urged protesting workers to return to their workplaces, assuring them that the process of determining the minimum wage would proceed through discussions.
It remains unclear what recommendations the newly formed board will make.

item.title: Shawkat Aziz Russell sent to jail in corruption case
item.description:
Shawkat Aziz Russell, son of late Partex Group founder-chairman M A Hashem, was sent to jail on Sunday after surrendering before a Dhaka court in a corruption case filed in 2017 over the allotment of plots under the Purbachal Residential Project.
Russell was sentenced to 14 years in prison in the case. He surrendered before the court of Judge Md Abdus Salam of Dhaka Special Judge Court-9 and sought bail, saying he intended to appeal against the verdict. The court rejected his bail application and ordered his imprisonment.
Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) prosecutor Khandaker Shamim Hossain confirmed the development.
On October 13, the same court sentenced 8 people, including Russell, to 14 years in prison each over the illegal allotment of 2 plots in Purbachal.
The other convicts are former Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha (Rajuk) chairman Iqbal Uddin Chowdhury, former Rajuk members SD Fayez, AKM Wahedul Islam, SM Jafar Ullah, HM Zahurul Haque and Md Rezaul Karim Tarafder, and Ashfaq Aziz Rubel, another son of M A Hashem.
According to the verdict, Russell and Ashfaq were each sentenced to 7 years of rigorous imprisonment under Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and another 7 years under Section 409 of the Penal Code.
They were also fined Tk20 lakh each, with an additional year of imprisonment in default of payment.
The 6 former Rajuk officials received the same prison sentences and fines.
The court ordered the sentences to run concurrently, with time already spent in custody to be deducted from the prison terms. The accused were acquitted of charges under Section 420 of the Penal Code, as the allegations under that section could not be proved.
The court also ordered the cancellation and confiscation of 2 plots, numbered 011 and 013, each measuring 10 kathas, on Road 405 in Sector 1 of Purbachal. The plots had been allotted to Russell and Ashfaq.
The ACC filed the case on February 8, 2017, alleging that the 2 plots, measuring 20 kathas in total, had been allotted to the brothers through abuse of influence and collusion with Rajuk officials, causing financial losses to the state.
The case was filed by then ACC Deputy Assistant Director Silvia Ferdous.

item.title: Binance heist: How were cryptocurrency billions stolen?
item.description:
Binance, the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange, estimates that assets worth $6.3 billion were impacted by a hacking attack against the trading platform.
But how was such a theft possible, and what does it reveal about the security of cryptocurrencies? AFP takes a look.
Binance, the world’s largest platform by digital currency trading volume, claims to have 335 million users.
That compares to the reported 741 million cryptocurrency owners worldwide cited by Crypto.com.
However, Binance has faced its fair share of scandals. Its former CEO, Changpeng Zhao, was convicted in the United States in 2024 for violating anti-money laundering laws, though he was later pardoned by President Donald Trump.
It has faced further US legal troubles, including being accused of selling assets that qualify as unregistered securities.
In France, Binance is suspected of having failed to meet its obligations regarding the oversight of client funds.
Having failed to obtain authorisation under the European Markets in Crypto Assets (MiCA) regulation, Binance recently announced a partial suspension of its operations within the European Union.
Cryptocurrencies are based on a technology called blockchain, a digital ledger that records transactions and is designed to make falsification particularly difficult.
Transfers are authorised using “private keys” -- long strings of characters kept secret. However, this does not fully protect funds from theft.
“Even when you think you are using one of the most robust exchanges in the world, it can still be hacked,” Stephane Ifrah, an analyst at Coinhouse, told AFP.
To gain access to private keys or the systems that authorise transfers, hackers can exploit a software vulnerability, deploy malicious software, or target individuals -- for instance through phishing.
Some keys are stored on hardware wallets that are not connected to the internet.
However, these devices are not immune to attacks. Funds belonging to users of the French firm Ledger were stolen after malicious components were inserted into devices sold by a third-party retailer.
In the case of Binance, the investigation is pointing toward a “compromised” laptop of one of its engineers, in addition to “points of breach”, the platform said on X.
While there has been no official confirmation, analyst firms TRM Labs, Chainalysis and Elliptic point to hackers linked to North Korea, specifically the group known as TraderTraitor or the “Lazarus Group”.
The amount purportedly stolen is four times the sum that the same hackers -- according to the FBI -- siphoned from the platform Bybit in February 2025.
That theft totalled $1.5 billion, which at the time was the largest ever cryptocurrency heist.
According to Elliptic and Chainalysis, some of the funds stolen from Binance have been traced to the same pool of assets as those taken in a recent hack of the platform Bitget, which the victim attributed to Pyongyang.
Binance says that around $3 billion of the affected crypto -- nearly half the total amount affected -- has been frozen with help from issuers and infrastructure partners.
But the freezing of assets does not mean the funds have been recovered.
According to Ifrah, the attackers could employ anonymisation tools, such as cryptocurrency “mixers” or “tumblers”, designed to make tracking the stolen assets more difficult.
Binance asserts that it will cover the losses resulting from the hack.
But as Ifrah states, “it is clear that there is no such thing as zero risk”.

item.title: CUET students call fresh shutdown over acting VC appointment
item.description:
Students of Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) have announced a fresh one-day shutdown for Monday, protesting the decision to assign Professor Kazi Delwar Hossain the vice-chancellor's routine duties for just one day.
The announcement comes shortly after students resumed classes and examinations following a prolonged academic shutdown.
The students announced the programme in an emergency statement issued on Sunday evening, alleging that the one-day arrangement had raised concerns over the university's administrative stability and academic environment.
They warned that further programmes would be announced if their demands and objections were not properly addressed.
During the shutdown, they will boycott all classes, examinations and administrative activities conducted under the one-day acting VC arrangement.
Earlier on Sunday afternoon, students staged a demonstration on the campus, protesting the decision.
According to university sources, CUET Vice-Chancellor Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam is scheduled to attend a meeting of the University Grants Commission (UGC) in Dhaka on Monday. In his absence, Professor Kazi Delwar Hossain, dean of the Faculty of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, has been assigned the vice-chancellor's routine administrative and academic responsibilities.
The decision was communicated through an email sent by the vice-chancellor on Sunday.
In the email, Sheikh Shariful Alam said he would be in Dhaka on November 2 to attend an official UGC meeting. To ensure the smooth continuation of the university's administrative and academic activities during his absence, Professor Delwar Hossain had been authorised to perform the vice-chancellor's routine duties alongside his own responsibilities, in accordance with the relevant statutory provisions.
The arrangement took effect on the afternoon of November 1 and will remain in force until the evening of November 2.
When contacted, Professor Kazi Delwar Hossain described the matter as a "regular issue" and declined to comment further.
Meanwhile, the newly appointed vice-chancellor, Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam, has yet to return to the campus since the Puja vacation, despite the resumption of regular working days.
On September 21, Professor Sheikh Shariful Alam of Khulna University of Engineering and Technology (KUET) was appointed CUET vice-chancellor, replacing Professor Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem.

item.title: Man stabbed to death in Dhaka’s Lalbagh
item.description:
A 35-year-old man was stabbed to death by some miscreants at Shahidnagar in Lalbagh area of the capital on Sunday.
The deceased was identified as Biplab alias Farma Biplab, a staff of a fish shop and son of Nazrul Islam of the area.
Three people appeared around 2pm near Baitul Fala Jam-e-Mosque in Shahidnagar area and stabbed him indiscriminately, leaving him dead on the spot, said Abdus Selim Mia, sub-inspector of Lalbagh Police Station.
On information, police recovered the body and sent it to Dhaka Medical College and Hospital morgue around 4:15pm.
Police said Biplab died due to excessive bleeding.
However, police are investigating the motive behind the killing and trying to arrest those involved in the killing, said SI Selim.

item.title: Tanti Dal leader hacked to death in Khulna
item.description:
A local leader of Jatiyatabadi Tanti Dal, an affiliate of BNP, was hacked to death at his business establishment in Khulna city’s Rayermahal area on Sunday evening.
The deceased was identified as Humayun Kabir, joint convener of Khulna city Tanti Dal and son of Syed Anwar Ali.
Police and local sources said a group of assailants attacked him with sharp weapons while he was sitting at his business establishment, ‘Hill Canteen’, behind Rayermahal Boro Mosque.
The assailants, armed with locally made weapons, ramdas and machetes, hacked him indiscriminately before fleeing the scene, leaving him critically injured.
He was rushed to Khulna Medical College Hospital, where doctors declared him dead.
Abu Saeed Sheikh, convener of the Khulna city Tanti Dal, confirmed that Kabir was the organisation’s joint convener.
“We are looking into the motive behind the killing,” he said.
Mizanur Rahman Milton, convener of the Khulna city BNP media cell, also confirmed Kabir’s political position and said he was hacked to death by assailants.
Kabir’s relatives have blamed local Chhatra Dal leaders for the killing.
His nephew, Syed Didarul Alam Biplob, alleged that the attack stemmed from a financial dispute with Arafat Hossain, convener of Chhatra Dal’s Ward 14 unit.
“A group led by Arafat Hossain attacked and hacked my uncle to death over a dispute involving money,” he said.
Kabir had contested the previous Khulna City Corporation election as a councillor from Ward 14 and was preparing to contest the upcoming KCC election from the same ward.
Syed Shahjahan Ali, officer-in-charge of Khalishpur Police Station, said the incident occurred in an area bordering Khalishpur and Aranghata Police Stations but fell under the jurisdiction of Aranghata police.
Aranghata Police Station OC Alimur Rahman said police had visited the scene and launched an investigation to identify those involved.
“Efforts are underway to identify and arrest those responsible,” he said.

item.title: Iran warns new war with US could last longer
item.description:
Iran warned on Sunday that any new war with the United States could last longer than the previous conflict and that US President Donald Trump would not be the one to determine its duration.
“A potential future war could last longer than previous conflict, and the American president would not be in a position to dictate the timing or the conditions of its conclusion,” said army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia, according to Iranian state television.
He was referring to the most intense phase of the fighting in the war that began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, killing the Islamic republic’s supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Iran responded by launching missiles and drones across the region, while the militant groups it backs also entered the fray in Lebanon and Yemen.
Iran’s Defense Minister Mehrdad Akhlaghi on Sunday warned of a “proportionate, decisive, and impactful response” to any attack on the country, according to state TV.
“Those who pose threats will not dictate the scope, timing, or consequences of Iran’s defensive response,” he added.
Also on Sunday, Hossein Mohebbi, the spokesperson of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, echoed the remarks made by the country’s new supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei in a written message the day before.
“In a conflict with America, there are no geographical limitations; a vast theatre has been defined for inflicting damage upon the enemy,” Mohebbi said, according to state TV.
US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the United States has knocked out much of Iran’s military but still has to “take care of” one or two targets.
“We’ve knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes,” Trump said.

item.title: France opens attempted murder probe after petrol bomb attack
item.description:
France has launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at security forces during a weekend protest in Paris, prosecutors told AFP on Sunday.
On Saturday, clashes erupted in Paris and some other cities after hundreds of thousands of people staged a third weekend of protests against soaring living costs.
The Paris police prefecture said that several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles, including a Molotov cocktail. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has decried an “extraordinary” level of violence from some rioters.
“Explosive devices were thrown at around 15 gendarmes as well as police officers,” the prosecutor’s office said on Sunday.
Gendarmes are military police officers who are part of the French armed forces.
Prosecutors said an investigation had been opened for “attempted murder of persons vested with public authority”.
Dramatic images, including AFP photos and video, showed a homemade incendiary device exploding at the feet of a security officer in eastern Paris, engulfing his lower body in flames.
An assessment of the injured was ongoing, prosecutors said, adding that the reported injuries include second-degree burns.
Initial complaints were expected to be filed on Sunday.
The gendarme struck by the Molotov cocktail told French television of the burns he suffered, describing “skin that stings” and a “rain” of projectiles thrown at his unit.
No suspects “have been arrested at this stage in connection with the incident”, the prosecutor’s office said, adding that investigators were working to identify those responsible.
Far-right leader Marine Le Pen said those responsible for the firebomb attack must be “punished with the utmost severity”, in a post on X, describing images of the officer in flames as “unbearable”.
More than 770 people were arrested during weekend protests in France, the interior ministry said on Sunday. The ministry said there had been “no major incidents” late on Saturday.
The number of shops damaged on the sidelines of Saturday’s protests was significantly lower than during previous weekends, with some 20 businesses affected, according to France’s Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).
But CCI France voiced concern about the impact of the protests on retail activity ahead of the year-end holiday season, a peak period for businesses.

item.title: Labour unrest hits 529 factories, nearly 987,000 workers absent
item.description:
Workers have walked out of 529 factories across the country's major industrial zones amid labour unrest, leaving nearly 987,000 workers absent from work. The unrest has hit Gazipur, Mymensingh, Savar and Ashulia hardest, with further incidents reported in Mirpur under the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) jurisdiction.
The figures, based on information available until 3:30pm on Sunday, cover 2,134 factories across five major industrial zones.
According to the data, 276 of the affected factories are in Gazipur and Mymensingh, 185 in Savar-Ashulia and Jirani, and 68 in the DMP area, all located in Mirpur.
No incidents of workers leaving factories or failing to report for duty were recorded in Narayanganj or Chittagong.
A breakdown of the figures shows that the Gazipur-Mymensingh industrial belt has 836 factories, of which 276 were affected by labour unrest. A total of 645,360 workers at these factories did not report for duty.
In Savar-Ashulia and Jirani, 185 of the 441 factories were affected, with 290,205 workers absent from work.
Of the 320 factories under the DMP jurisdiction, 68 in Mirpur were affected, with 51,625 workers failing to report for duty.
Meanwhile, the data covers 197 factories in Narayanganj and 340 in Chittagong, with no worker walkouts or absenteeism reported in either area.
The report lists 1,816 factories as operational across the five industrial zones, while 529 were reportedly shut due to labour unrest.
Gazipur and Mymensingh recorded the highest number of workers absent from work, followed by Savar-Ashulia and Jirani. Together, these two industrial belts accounted for the largest share of the unrest.

item.title: Hili potters turn to innovative clay products to stay competitive
item.description:
Potters in Hakimpur upazila’s Hili area are diversifying their products, making modern clay mosquito coil holders and other decorative and household items to keep pace with changing consumer preferences and compete with plastic and melamine goods.
During a visit to Kumar Para in Chandipur village near the Hili border on Sunday, local potters said they were introducing innovative designs and attractive products to preserve their ancestral profession as demand for traditional earthenware declined.
The artisans are now producing household utensils and decorative items with colourful finishes and polished designs. Among their newer products, clay mosquito coil holders have gained popularity among customers.
Potters Yogesh Roy and Arati Bala said declining sales of traditional clay pots and pans had forced them to explore alternative products. They said the coil holders had become popular because customers considered them a safer option for burning mosquito coils.
Demand also rises during power outages, when mosquitoes become a nuisance and people rely on coils at night, they added.
Md Khademul Haque, a resident of Bagmara village in Hakimpur, said he previously had no dedicated container for burning mosquito coils and had to place them on plates or other household items.
“I like the clay coil holder because it has a lid and a stand for placing the coil,” he said.
The newly designed holders feature perforated lids that allow smoke to escape and central stands to hold the coils. Some can accommodate several coils at a time.
Potter Bimal Pal said innovation was essential for traditional artisans to survive competition from plastic products.
“Unless we introduce new products, it will be difficult for us to survive in competition with plastic goods,” he said.
He added that the holders were designed to contain burning coils and falling ash, helping reduce the risk of fire spreading.
Another potter, Anik Pal, said they had recently expanded production to include decorated drinking glasses, buckets of different sizes and plates.
The artisans are using attractive designs to appeal to customers, particularly younger buyers, who increasingly purchase clay products for decoration and as hobby items.
Anik said growing interest in the new products had brought some relief to local potters and renewed their hopes of sustaining their traditional craft.
The potters have urged the government to provide support to sustain the pottery industry.
Dinajpur Sadar Upazila Social Services Officer Md Mainul Islam said there is no specific government project aimed at supporting the pottery industry.
However, the Ministry of Social Welfare provides assistance to members of the pottery community through various social welfare programmes, including old-age allowances, medical assistance and financial grants.
He said he had learned that the government was considering launching specific projects to support and preserve the traditional pottery industry.
He added that various government departments were already providing support to the sector in different ways.
